Unhack, developed and published by InvertMouse, is a creative fusion of visual novel storytelling and light puzzle gameplay that blends science fiction themes with a distinctive anime-inspired style. The game places players in the role of an “Unhacker,” a digital security expert tasked with combating a destructive virus known as the 5K Worm. Set in a futuristic cyberspace where artificial intelligence and human ingenuity coexist, Unhack tells a story that explores the ethics of technology, corporate greed, and the human relationship with digital consciousness. At its heart, it’s a compact but thoughtful experience that aims to deliver both emotional storytelling and gameplay engagement within a short runtime.

From the first moments, Unhack establishes an energetic rhythm that sets it apart from typical visual novels. It intersperses dialogue-driven scenes with interactive puzzle segments that simulate the process of “unhacking” a corrupted system. These puzzles take the form of grid-based mazes, where players must guide a digital avatar through pathways filled with hazards, timing movements to avoid viruses, lasers, or other obstacles. The mechanics are simple and intuitive, relying on observation and timing rather than reflex-heavy gameplay. This structure creates a balance between passive reading and active engagement, preventing the narrative from becoming too static. Each completed level unlocks more story segments, making progress feel tangible while maintaining an approachable difficulty curve.

The game’s visual presentation is minimalistic but expressive. Character designs are stylized in a clean, anime-inspired fashion, with sharp lines and vivid colors that contrast nicely against the darker digital backdrops. Although the environments are not highly detailed, the art direction succeeds in establishing a futuristic mood. Each scene feels like a glimpse into a glowing virtual world where data flows like rivers of light. The simplicity of the visuals also helps maintain clarity during the puzzle sections, ensuring the player’s focus remains on navigation and timing. The overall aesthetic feels cohesive, leaning into its indie roots while embracing the charm of an interactive anime episode.

A major strength of Unhack lies in its voice acting and music. Every primary character is voiced, bringing personality and nuance to the dialogue. The protagonist’s AI companion, Weedy, is particularly memorable—her lively and sometimes naïve demeanor contrasts nicely with the colder, more pragmatic tone of other artificial intelligences encountered throughout the story. The performances lend weight to moments that might otherwise have felt flat on the page, adding warmth and tension to exchanges that reveal the story’s underlying moral questions. The soundtrack complements this dynamic well, alternating between calm electronic ambience and more urgent, fast-paced tracks that heighten tension during puzzle sequences. The synergy between sound and dialogue helps give the game an emotional core that transcends its technical simplicity.

Narratively, Unhack delivers a concise but engaging tale about human ambition and the consequences of technological overreach. As the player digs deeper into the cyber warfare between Smash Security and the 5K Worm, the story introduces philosophical questions about identity and self-awareness in artificial intelligence. It explores the fine line between creation and control, as well as the moral cost of exploiting digital life for corporate gain. The writing isn’t overly complex, but it maintains enough intrigue and pacing to keep players invested from start to finish. What stands out most is its sincerity—the story feels written from a place of genuine curiosity and empathy rather than cynicism, making its themes more approachable than abstract.

The gameplay, while engaging, remains limited in scope. The maze-based hacking sequences evolve only slightly over the course of the story, introducing minor variations but not enough to significantly alter the experience. They serve more as narrative devices than as standalone challenges, breaking up the flow of dialogue while reinforcing the theme of “repairing” digital corruption. For players accustomed to deep puzzle mechanics or long campaigns, the simplicity may feel underwhelming. Yet this restraint also works in the game’s favor, keeping the focus on character interaction and atmosphere rather than mechanical difficulty. It’s clear that the game’s primary ambition is emotional connection rather than technical mastery.

Despite its brief length—lasting only a few hours—Unhack manages to create a satisfying arc. It doesn’t overstay its welcome, and its pacing ensures that each scene feels purposeful. The story’s emotional peaks come from moments of reflection rather than spectacle, particularly in the evolving bond between the protagonist and his AI companions. There’s a surprising amount of heart in the writing, and by the time the credits roll, the player is left with a sense of quiet contemplation rather than exhaustion. It’s an experience designed to linger in thought, not through complexity, but through its simple, human approach to science fiction storytelling.

From a technical perspective, the game runs smoothly and is accessible to nearly any system. It loads quickly, saves reliably, and features a user interface that is clean and easy to navigate. While the visual novel framework is basic, it accomplishes its goals without distraction. The minimalist menus and clear visual feedback make it approachable even for those unfamiliar with the genre. This accessibility, combined with its short runtime and affordable price, makes Unhack an easy recommendation for players looking for a compact, narrative-driven experience that doesn’t demand heavy investment.

Ultimately, Unhack succeeds by knowing exactly what it wants to be. It doesn’t aspire to be a sprawling epic or a deeply intricate puzzle game; instead, it delivers a focused, heartfelt experience that merges narrative and interactivity with elegance. Its charm lies in its sincerity—the way it invites players into a futuristic world not to overwhelm them, but to make them think about the relationship between human creators and their digital counterparts. Though its mechanics are simple and its runtime short, the story’s emotional resonance and presentation make it memorable long after completion. Unhack is a reminder that even small-scale games can explore big ideas, offering both warmth and reflection in a sleek, digital shell.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

I have a special appreciation for visual novels that are interwoven with gameplay. This one certainly doesn't disappoint in that category!
The mini-game style gameplay requires you to find the right timing. It's not overly difficult, I played on Hard (three lives) for all of the missions without issue. Each level builds upon the previous ones and has a new mechanic added keeping it fresh.
However what I found a bit inconventient was how the story gets auto-played by passing certain level points which leads to two outcomes. Either you naturally breeze through like I initially did and have to back up the dialogue at the end to read it or you have to periodically stop to read each piece of dialogue as it comes up. It's not that big a problem and I have no idea how to solve this for an ideal flow, though I believe I should at least mention it.
Nevertheless the story is quite nice and did get me a little emotional over the AI characters at the end.
Due to how short it is it doesn't go very deep into the subject matter present and isn't particularly complex, but in combination with the gameplay, the nice visuals and great sound design it is a good, simple game for an evening.
To sum it up, each piece comes together to make a quite good game I recommend.

A fairly short title combining action puzzles with visual novel sections. Is the idea of virus chasing enticing enough?

As an 'unhacking' specialist you are tasked with worm elimination. The task boils down to simple navigation of simple maze -like stages in order to exterminate computer worms or to reach certain places. There are ten stages within the main game and three extra in the DLC. You can select any stage from the start. Also, there are three levels of difficulty but even the hardest one doesn't pose any serious challenge. As for the story, while all stages contain some chatting sections, most talking occurs between levels. It is a fairly short and straightforward sci-fi story with mostly predictable events. There is only one ending so one playthrough is enough to see everything. Due to its length, characters are underdeveloped and some parts remain unanswered but it still is decent enough to enjoy. For the price asked, and when compared to similar titles at this price point, it is good enough to fill a few hours of your day.

The main theme here is sci-fi, or virtual space to be more specific, and it is more than clear. Stages look like electronic circuits and cold colours emphasise this style. Everything feels a bit sterile and somewhat empty, budget-like. Characters done in anime style also reflect the low budget as it's at best average. Still, overall design and visual quality is acceptable.

Electronic music is one of the strongest points of this game. I really enjoyed some tracks and the free soundtrack DLC is a cool bonus. There is also some voice acting which is unusual for such a cheap title, however, it is pretty bland. Character voices do not convey emotions well and sound pretty monotone. Not terrible but unnecessary feature.

No bugs encountered. 

To summarise, a short action puzzle/visual novel with average anime art and decent soundtrack. If you enjoy the listed genres you might find it enjoyable but it is still a budget title so low expectations are almost a must: 5.1/10

This is a fun little game. Kind of short, but fun.

[b]Visuals[/b]:
There's a little awkwardness in the sprites, but they're okay. The rest of the game visuals are better, and that's usually what you're focusing on anyway.

[b]Voice Acting[/b]:
The voices are a bit awkward. There are awkward pauses, and sometimes their tone seems a little strange for what they're saying. It's definitely not the strong suit of this game.

[b]Characters[/b]:
I'd have liked to have more time with the characters, as the game seemed to move a little fast. The characters had different personalities, but kind of started to feel the same after a while.

[b]Story[/b]:
The story's okay. It didn't really wow me in any way, but I started to feel bad at the end, so it gets some points there.

[b]Comedy[/b]:
There was a lot of comedy in this game, and it was clearly (at least to me it was) inspired by what you find in anime. They voice acting added to some, and took away from others. If you enjoy this kind of humor, it's going to be really funny, but I personally wasn't drawn to it.

[b]Gameplay[/b]:
The gameplay's simplistic, but I think that's a good thing. It plays in a way that's simple to get the hang of, but it still manages to provide a challenge later in the game.

[b]Music[/b]:
I think the music is the best part of the game. It acts as a decent background drone that matches the overall tone of the game. I think the only possible improvement that could be made is better transitions. The music seems to suddenly shift, and it's kind of off putting.

[b]Conclusion[/b]:
It's not great, but it's fun. The DLC adds a short backstory, that helps you understand A2 a little more, but I think is too short to have much of an emotional impact, though the same can be said for the main game as well. Can't see myself playing it more, but I'm glad I played it the one time.

While this game is rough, it holds a lot of potential. I think i'ts one of the most inovative Visual Novels I've ever seen. I played it a long time ago and felt like coming back and as I am now writing this piece, I think it deserves some attention.

As I said, it is not a smooth ride, the "hacking" mechanic is also used to advance text, which means that more action-y players won't feel as bored as if just reading a story, they can actually watch it unfold and that depends on their reaction and planning. The puzzles aren't very complex, and you can always go with difficulty settings that give you three lives or none at all, nothing will impact the story, its just a way you can challenge yourself a little.

And speaking of the story, I believe it is fairly nice. Nothing too write home about, but very touching and dramatic, with a few twists here and there. Despite the fact that there is little to no introduction, As long as you read the sinopsis on the store page, you will be fine.

Another high point is a respectable work with sound design and voice acting too. On the visual style, while the mugshots are cute, the gameplay design is very minimalistic, but it tells you just enough that you need to know. The only major bad part I can think of is the way the game is programmed, not allowing you to change resolution nor take screenshots. There are ways to circumvent this though, though that work should be a point. Also, for a visual novel, the lack of a gallery really hurts it, and it has rather impressive art between episodes.

Unhack is probably one of the first games I've seen from this creator, and I've played a couple more. I will say again that it is a rough start but a very well crafted one. It shows great promise and despite its shortcomings I still have to praise it for what it does. Can't wait to see what its sequel will bring.

Unhack, a VN about a slightly perverted "unhacker", his female AI partner, and their adventures as they battle the forces of internet viruses.

[b]Graphics: 4/10[/b]

Right off the bat, the game comes across as rather lackluster. Characters are expressive and the art style is consistent, maintaining the mood throughout, but backgrounds are exceedingly basic, while CGs are few, rather poor compared to the regular graphics, and only thinly connected to the plot.

[b]Sound: 5/10[/b]

Unlike most indie VNs nowadays, this one is fully voice acted, and pretty well to boot. Sadly, it's matched by a fairly forgettable OST; it's... there, it just doesn't do much of anything.

[b]Story: 6/10[/b]

The core of a good VN is its story, and here is where Unlink is at its weirdest: on one hand, the plot has lots of twists throughout its meager length, unusual enough to be surprising but not so much as to strain credibility, which keeps things interesting. But on the other, it [i]is[/i] rather short, which means there's next to no world building and very little development for any of its characters.

[b]Longevity: 0/10[/b]

A bit over an hour for both the main game and its DLC, with no branching whatsoever outside the failure screen for dying at the minigame that forms the core of its gameplay; which, while fun enough, offers no reason to replay once solved.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

So, nothing really stands out besides the voice acting, and even that is mostly by the standards of indie VNs. But even so, I enjoyed it; perhaps it's the uniqueness of its premise, or simply the fact that nothing in it manages to overstay its welcome. It feels like a really focused labor of love from start to finish, if that makes sense.

Still, even at its regular low price I'd have trouble recommending it; the value is just not there. But on sale, or thought of as a small donation to an indie dev, I do believe it's worth a buy: in spite of its flaws its got plenty of charm and, as the saying goes, I could think of worse ways to spend a lazy afternoon. Or maybe just a quiet moment during one.

Think of this game less of a VN and more of a quick puzzle game with some VN elements and excellent voice acting. The story, while short, did pique my interest long enough for me to clear the whole game (which takes around an hour or less). It also provides some decent backstory for its sequel, Unhack 2. It's nothing deep, however.

Gameplay is basically sliding block puzzles. You move across a maze of sorts with WASD and try to get the other side, sometimes while avoiding lasers and killing enemies through use of timed shots. The game isn't hard at all, and Easy mode even gives you infinite lives. It does get a little stale though, and I would've liked to see more intricate hazards.

There's no saving feature. That said, you're allowed to choose which "episode" you want to play at the title screen, so the saving isn't really needed (each episode lasts around 5-10 minutes depending on how fast you clear). I would've liked an indicator of what episode I was currently playing, but it's not that hard to quit and choose a different one if you select wrong.

The voice acting is superb. Probably the biggest name here is Xanthe Huynh of K-On, SAO, Persona 5 fame. That's not to say that the other actresses didn't do good jobs. Aimee Smith, Skylar Davenport, Rachael Messer, and Xanthe all performed wonderfully at bringing the characters to life, despite how short the game is.

I really do recommend Unhack. Maybe not at the 3.99 price point for something this short and a bit rough around the edges, but at a lower price I do suggest buying this game.

Unhack è una visual novel/puzzle game stupenda! Il doppiaggio è di ottimo livello, perfetto per ogni personaggio, ognuno dei quali è caratterizzato alla perfezione. La grafica è semplice, ma d'effetto. Viene fatto un sapiente uso dei colori, facendoci capire sempre come ci dobbiamo muovere. E le musiche... mamma mia, le musiche! Assolutamente stupende! Soprattutto, secondo me, quella del livello 4 (chiamata "High Stakes"). Il compositore è stato veramente bravo a comporre ogni singolo brano, ognuno dei quali è assolutamente perfetto per il momento in cui viene utilizzato. Così come i suoni. Il character design dei personaggi è realizzato davvero bene. E poi... la storia. Mamma mia, la storia! Si evolve in modo perfetto, partendo come una cosa semplice ed evolvendo in qualcosa di assurdo! Scritta davvero bene! L'unica piccola pecca è il fatto che vi siano, purtroppo, solo 10 livelli. Però la rigiocabilità è data dalla possibilità di scegliere fra 3 livelli di difficoltà: Normale, Difficile, e la Folle. Quest'ultima in particolare trovo sia l'essenza vera e propria del gioco. Perché a questa difficoltà vi assicuro che non sarà difficile incorrere nel Game Over. Inoltre, il DLC "Unhack: Destruction" aggiunge 3 livelli extra, basati su un altro personaggio, approfondendo la sua storia. E trovo che sia davvero un buon DLC! In pratica, fra gioco principale e DLC spendereste 5 euro. Quasi nulla, insomma, dato che li vale tranquillamente tutti! Sono inoltre scaricabili (tutto da Steam, dato che non l'ho detto) le Soundtrack gratuitamente, ed anche l'Artbook Digitale a 2 euro, se vi interessa (a me sì). Quindi, che aspettate?? Compratelo! Intro: When I joined Steam in 2012, my first attempt at VNs (visual novels) and A.I. storylines was Analogue- A Hate Story and Hate Plus. I discovered Unhack shortly thereafter and I can say with certainty that InvertMouse's series is the more accessible of the two. Both make my recommendation list for VNs that I would recommend to newcomers, but if they approach this after being introduced to anime or manga, Unhack is better.

Pros: [list]
[*] The narrative (while simple) is the foundation for the sequel which genuinely surprised me in the direction it went. Despite that it still respects the story of this original and provides time to feel closure and emotional punch to the story from the first. (And on a narrative note, there is prequel DLC which has a separate review from me. Highly recommended and referenced [spoiler] as a location and art gallery in the sequel. It also makes one particular moment that much sadder and emotional when compared to another reunion in Unhack 2.[/spoiler] 
[*] The art, while simple still impresses during the wallpaper sections and makes narrative sense when you consider A.I. have multiple generations. This improves the effect in the sequel, which has even better wallpapers and a new artist mimic and contrast the old style using pixels, low-res vs. high-res images, and some impressive color work.
[*] Short length so it won't take too many hours out of your life (Unlike some MUCH longer VNs. Looking at you Sunrider).
[*] Gameplay is simple but requires some skill closer to the end. More interactive than the usual VN, which I appreciate. Plus it provides story during gameplay which is something that dual-genre VNs don't often have (looking at you Sunrider).
[*] Has optional voice acting with actresses who have been in several anime dubs post 2010 till now (Xanthe Huynh especially for voicing Menma in Anohana and Haru in Persona 5). And if you don't like voice work in your VNs check the options.
[/list]
Cons (or Meh points): [list]
[*] Short length threw me off when I played the sequel which is double the length. However, it needed the time to provide closure and was better for it.
[*] Soundtrack (Which is now available for free) is respectable but didn't stand out. The following soundtrack has significant improvements, but both are nice to listen to.
[/list] 

Summary: Thank you InvertMouse for making the foundation for what the sequel and this series achieved. Here's hoping the future is full of friendly A.I. who aren't comprised of HAL, GLaDOS, Wheatley, SHODAN, and the Sibyl System. [spoiler](Those five would terrify the hell out of me[/spoiler]. Keep up the great work and I look forward to The Last Birdling and Without Within 3.

This short kinetic visual novel feature an anonymous male protagonist referred to as The Unhacker. As the best unhacker of Smash Security, the Unhacker attempts to investigate the source of the 5K Worm virus infection that is spreading across cyberspace with some help from his AI companions Weedy and Miss Debug. Suspecting their immediate competitor ACME Antivirus to be behind the creation and spread of the virus for financial gain and profit, the Unhacker attempts to hack across multiple different security systems in the form of 10 arcade puzzle/action minigames which involve moving a square icon across a maze to an exit without being destroyed by various environmental hazards and uncovers a sinister past on Smash Security and The Unhacker himself before confronting the source of the 5K Worm.

Although the arcade minigames can be played at varying difficulty with infinite retries and infinite health in allies at the easiest difficulty, it would be nice if the game allows the take screenshot button on Steam to work, as well as a gallery to list and show all unlocked CGs instead of having to replay a particular chapter and its minigame to obtain the CG. Having dialogue over various parts in the arcade minigame which often automatically skip when moving across the arcade minigame quickly to avoid the environmental hazards which move in real-time draw attention away from the storyline and plot. Soundtracks and overall game presentation is good after factoring in soundtracks and voiced dialogue. Recommended when at sale or in bundle discount as it takes less than 10 hours to finish all arcade minigames and read through the entire visual novel.

A short game with simple gameplay, but a nice distraction when everything is said & done.

It's inexpensive, moreso when on sale (full disclosure, I got it on sale, so under $3 for the game & it's extra content) but it also only took me about 2 hours to go through the game.  Still, that's a better dollar/hour rate than going to the movies, so I'm not going to say much else about the length of the game.

The gameplay is simple, which is kinda nice in this insatance (especially considering it's a simple graphical representation of you being a super white-hat hacker [or, as the game calls it "unhacker"] via a colored square moving along a path)  You use WASD, clicking with your mouse (I do not suggest using the mouse for the "unhacking" bits) or the number pad to control your little square, moving from point A to point B (though you usually stop along at points C F and P along the way) to achieve whatever goal the story put before you during each segment (episode)  Sometimes there are enemies to avoid, sometimes there are traps to avoid.  There are some pickups, and eventually some things you activate to move things along.  Simple in execution, but with enough added as you play to keep it interesting (I was interested enough to blow through in one sitting, so take what you will from that)

The story is solid enough for what it is.  It's all given through conversations between your character & the various AI's you work with (and their conversations with each other) and all the AI's have full voiceovers, which are pretty nice.  It's a simple story, and I think that works in it's favor here.  The story & gameplay mesh pretty nicely here.  There were a couple little twists here & there, but with how things progressed they weren't terribly suprising.  Not bad, but nothing to write home about.

As far as the art goes, it's nice.  It sticks to standard VN art with the characters having only a few images during gameplay, with most changes simply being expressions, but that art is clean & seems to fit well with everything else in the game.  After each level you get a screen that somehow relates to what just happened in the story, and they all look well done for a title from such a small group.  I didn't dislike anything that was presented to me on my screen.

The music works very well as game music.  It never gets overly distracting, fits the mood of the levels well, and is able to go on for a while with a smooth loop that won't suddenly jolt you with a harsh transition.  I will say that the stage cleared music (played while the cleared screen image is up) doesn't always feel right with the story elements of the game.  Not a deal breaker by a long shot, but just me stating my opinion.

All in all, I'm satisfied with my purchase and will keep an eye out for other stuff from these folks.  It's short enough to play in a single sitting, and interesting enough to keep your interest long enough to achieve that.  I'll probably go back and try a playthrough on the hardest mode in a bit (I only played on Hard, since it was midnight and I had just gotten off of work) but that'll be for another day.

Although it looks like a game from Japan, this was not made there (I believe) and therefore the creators could enter the English-speaking market easily. You get to discover a new world in this game. The voice acting is funny at times, as Miss Debug always says "*Yawnies*". The voice acting is on point.

The DLC for this game is even shorter than the main game, with only three levels to complete. It shows of a sad story of ACME Security's history, and actually made me feel a little bit emotional for the characters. The gameplay here is basic though, with this focus being on story. If this DLC were to be longer, I would have definitely cried from the sadness.

Overall, an excellent game. And for the price, it's a good game. You should only play this game in one sitting, as you may lose track on which level that you are on. The game is just for the story.

Unhack has a beautiful art style, kawaii AI girls with cute voice acting, and an interesting theme and story.

This is an entertaining and interesting mix of a puzzle game and a visual novel. It is short but masterfully paced. The short running time enables the creators to keep surprising you with changes and with delightful interplay of mechanics, story, art, voice acting and music. They all develop together and play off each other in smart and satisfying ways. It also helps that the game is very easy so you're never stuck in one place.

There is no one aspect of this game that is very good. The story is clichéd, the mechanics simplistic, the art repetitive and the humour juvenile. But they all work together perfectly and reinforce each other. The game is so full of smart ideas and genuine enthusiasm that even its flaws become charming. This is a short, unique experience that's easy to recommend.

Unhack features simplistic puzzle gameplay over a backdrop of visual novel -esque dialogue and character interraction.  The dialogue is the main "pro" of the game, but it also acts as its main "con."  

The three AI characters are all voice acted, but the protagonist isn't  This means that while you're progressing through the puzzles, you'll need to look down to read the protagonist's dialogue in order to gain context for what the AI voice actors are saying to you.  This really takes you out of the puzzles in the worst way.  It would have been better if the protagonist had been voice acted as well to create a better flow between the puzzles and story.  WIthout this, you have to tackle to puzzles slower than you would normally in order to experience the full story as well.  This disn't prevent me from having fun with the game, it just stood out as a main issue that could have been prevented.  

All in all, it's still a fun little game that's worth the price if you're looking for a casual one-off experience.

At its core, its a simple, linear, and short game, and nothing else should be expected of it.  A lot of things in this game feel really cheesy and mediocre though, even with that in mind.  Honestly, it was kind of boring.  It was cheap though, so its to be expected.


The final boss fight was kinda cool, but not worth the playthrough.

The characters are cliche' and have shallow, if not non-existent, character development.  Characters appearing for the sake of appearing, villians being there solely for being a conflict rather than anything that feels menacing, etc.  Plot is very simple, you'll see pretty much everything from a mile off after the first 5 minutes or so.  Nothing is explained and there is little to no worldbuilding.  Many things just happen for the sake of happening, especially with character and villian appearances.

Gameplay is essentially navigating a linear maze dodging obstacles all with timing-gimmicks.  Simple stuff, got kind of boring after the first hour.

Voice-acting was an interesting addition, and I admit I bought into the game because of the premise of amateur voice acting in an indie game.  However, it was too monotone; I never really felt any emotion come out of the characters, it was as if they were just reading the text that appeared on the screen to you.  Nevertheless, I have to give them points for trying.


At the end of the day, the game felt like a poor time filler and I expected more replayability, but I knew what I was buying into.  If you are bored and want something to fill an hour or two, go ahead and get this game.  However, its experience is short lived and forgetable.  There are many other cheap games on steam and ways to fill your time in them.  As such, I do not recommend this title.
